episode_summary: Hashing It Out interview with Paul Sztorc of LayerTwo Labs on DriveChain (BIP300/BIP301) as a permissionless sidechain approach to Bitcoin scaling, with his critiques of Lightning and of the 2015-2017 block size war, his account of SPV mining, the soft-fork activation logjam, and fee-economics predictions for L1 and L2.

cards.claim: Paul Sztorc said BIP300 and BIP301 together are known as DriveChain.
cards.speaker: Paul Sztorc
cards.quote: One of those ideas became BIP300 and another one became BIP301. And collectively, those are known as DriveChain.

cards.claim: Paul Sztorc explained that BIP301 blind merge mining lets miners earn sidechain fees without running the sidechain node.
cards.speaker: Paul Sztorc
cards.quote: So in blind merge mining, you don't need to run anything other than the L1 node.

cards.claim: Paul Sztorc described merged mining as a miner finding blocks for two chains at once with no additional hashing work.
cards.speaker: Paul Sztorc
cards.quote: a miner can find two blocks, a block for different blockchains all at the same time with no additional work.

cards.claim: Paul Sztorc said he published DriveChain in November 2015.
cards.speaker: Paul Sztorc
cards.quote: And I published DriveChain in November 2015.

cards.claim: Paul Sztorc said he published an essay called Measuring Decentralization in September 2015.
cards.speaker: Paul Sztorc
cards.quote: in september 2015 i had published an essay called measuring decentralization

cards.claim: Paul Sztorc said the orphan rate fell back to zero by 2015 after miners worked around the latency of validating full blocks.
cards.speaker: Paul Sztorc
cards.quote: But by 2015, it had already crashed back down to zero because the miners had already set to work solving this problem.

cards.claim: Paul Sztorc said miners started using SPV mining, switching to the next block before validating it, to cut corners.
cards.speaker: Paul Sztorc
cards.quote: the miners started to cut corners and cheat they use spv and spy mining to just switch to the next block without validating it at all.

cards.claim: Paul Sztorc said Satoshi got almost everything right but wrongly assumed every miner would run a full node.
cards.speaker: Paul Sztorc
cards.quote: I think Satoshi got almost everything right, but there's one thing he didn't quite get right

cards.claim: Paul Sztorc calculated that losing a few seconds of block time is roughly a 20% loss of revenue efficiency for a miner.
cards.speaker: Paul Sztorc
cards.quote: So losing a few seconds actually is like a minus 20% loss of revenue efficiency.

cards.claim: Paul Sztorc said the whole idea of sidechains is that users run whichever sidechain node they want, so miners do not need to run it.
cards.speaker: Paul Sztorc
cards.quote: the whole idea of sidechains is the users run whichever sidechain node they want.

cards.claim: Paul Sztorc said Ethereum's daily fees were in the millions of dollars, with a seven-day average of about 2.3 million.
cards.speaker: Paul Sztorc
cards.quote: Ethereum's daily fees are millions of dollars a day

cards.claim: Paul Sztorc argued that 51% hashrate can already interfere with every L2 because it already controls every L1.
cards.speaker: Paul Sztorc
cards.quote: 51% hashrate can already interfere with every L2.

cards.claim: Paul Sztorc said Lightning node operators or Ark super nodes collect L2 fees, whereas under BIP300 the miners would collect them.
cards.speaker: Paul Sztorc
cards.quote: The Lightning node operator is going to collect the fee, or the Arc Super node is going to collect the fee.

cards.claim: Paul Sztorc said L1 fees were usually about $400,000 a day, much less than the roughly $2.3 million a day in Ethereum L2-style fees he cited.
cards.speaker: Paul Sztorc
cards.quote: which are usually like $400,000 a day or something like that

cards.claim: Paul Sztorc predicted L1 fees would stay around 500,000 a day while total L2 transactions could grow to planetary scale very quickly.
cards.speaker: Paul Sztorc
cards.quote: l1 fees on the future will stay at around 500 000 but the l2 the total number of l2 transactions I think could grow to a planetary scale very, very quickly.

cards.claim: Paul Sztorc predicted there would eventually be a conflict in which miners make themselves the L2 because L2 fees would be far higher than L1 fees.
cards.speaker: Paul Sztorc
cards.quote: And so there will eventually be some kind of conflict.

cards.claim: Paul Sztorc said sidechains would let Bitcoin reach planetary scale in a non-ideal form, giving eight billion people a UTXO and Zcash-level privacy.
cards.speaker: Paul Sztorc
cards.quote: the idea allows Bitcoin to have planetary scale in some form not the ideal form but it gives 8 billion people

cards.claim: Paul Sztorc said Bitcoin miners only very recently learned about the DriveChain idea, around July of the previous year.
cards.speaker: Paul Sztorc
cards.quote: the Bitcoin miners only very recently found out about this idea as of like July or something.

cards.claim: Paul Sztorc predicted that Lightning needing more soft forks would break the soft-fork logjam in Bitcoin.
cards.speaker: Paul Sztorc
cards.quote: and now with Lightning needing more soft forks in order to work, that will probably break a lot of the logjam of the soft fork.

cards.claim: Paul Sztorc said SegWit took about 20 months from when it was first proposed to when it was coded.
cards.speaker: Paul Sztorc
cards.quote: it took segwit 20 months from when

cards.claim: Paul Sztorc said Bitcoin did something like 16 or 17 soft forks in its first seven years, and only SegWit and Taproot since then.
cards.speaker: Paul Sztorc
cards.quote: In the first seven years of Bitcoin's existence, we did something like 16 or 17 different soft forks.

cards.claim: Paul Sztorc said Taproot was proposed in January 2018 and not activated until November 2021, 46 months later.
cards.speaker: Paul Sztorc
cards.quote: It was activated, but it wasn't until November 2021, 46 months.

cards.claim: Paul Sztorc said miners' guilt over SegWit2x is a big barrier to activating the drivechain soft fork.
cards.speaker: Paul Sztorc
cards.quote: So that is all because of guilt over Segway2x

cards.claim: Paul Sztorc argued soft forks are not a risk because a soft fork does not change the protocol for anyone running a node.
cards.speaker: Paul Sztorc
cards.quote: because a soft work does not change the protocol for anyone who's running a node

cards.claim: Paul Sztorc argued that the victory in the block size war created many of Bitcoin's later problems.
cards.speaker: Paul Sztorc
cards.quote: So all of the biggest problems in Bitcoin were actually created as a result of our victory in the box size war.

cards.claim: Paul Sztorc predicted that Namecoin and prediction markets would be huge, with one name serving as a person's identity everywhere.
cards.speaker: Paul Sztorc
cards.quote: But I think honestly, Namecoin and prediction markets, those will be huge.

cards.claim: Paul Sztorc said he had predicted that darknet markets would decentralise into middlemen and Telegram bots.
cards.speaker: Paul Sztorc
cards.quote: I predicted that the darknet markets, since all they do is introduce the buyer and seller to each other

cards.claim: Paul Sztorc said the Canadian truckers protest showed that Bitcoin did not work for protest funding, because the government confiscated the Bitcoin.
cards.speaker: Paul Sztorc
cards.quote: And what we did is we just showed everyone that it didn't work.

cards.claim: Paul Sztorc summed up drivechains in ten words as devs competing and users winning.
cards.speaker: Paul Sztorc
cards.quote: When devs compete, users win.

cards.claim: The host argued that L1 chains are essentially different countries that will never agree on one global currency.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: all these L1s are essentially different countries.

title: Paul Sztorc of LayerTwo Labs | Drivechains, Scaling Bitcoin without Compromise
